## For waiting: threading and asyncio {#tools-waiting}

::: {.cards .two}

::: {.card}
[Threads: `threading`]{.card-title}
Several threads share one process and its memory. Python's lock, the **GIL**, lets one thread run Python code at a
time, so threads overlap waits, not work. The easy way in: a thread pool from `concurrent.futures`.

```{=html}
<pre class="type diagram" style="width:auto; font-size:0.8em; margin:12px 0 0; padding:14px 16px">with ThreadPoolExecutor(8) as ex:
    pages = list(ex.map(fetch, urls))</pre>
```
:::

::: {.card}
[One thread, many waits: `asyncio`]{.card-title}
An event loop runs functions that pause at `await` while they wait, and runs another one meanwhile. Thousands of
waits at once, with async libraries such as httpx.

```{=html}
<pre class="type diagram" style="width:auto; font-size:0.8em; margin:12px 0 0; padding:14px 16px">async def main():
    jobs = [fetch(u) for u in urls]
    return await asyncio.gather(*jobs)
pages = asyncio.run(main())</pre>
```
:::

:::

::: {.card .red}
[Not today: a forest fire computes; it doesn't wait.]{.card-title} Reach for these when your program mostly waits on
the network or the disk: downloads, web APIs, databases.
:::

::: {.notes}
- NumPy, pandas and other compiled libraries release the GIL inside their heavy loops, so threads can speed those up.
  Pure Python code, like our forest fire, can't.
- Python 3.14 makes the free-threaded build officially supported, but it is still a separate, optional install.
- asyncio helps only when every slow call is async-aware (httpx, aiohttp, asyncpg). One blocking call stalls the loop.
:::

## For computing: multiprocessing {#tools-computing}

::: {.small}
Separate processes, each with its own memory and its own Python, compute at the same time. The cost: starting them,
and sending inputs and results between them.
:::

| In code | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| `pool.map(run, tasks)` [today]{.pill} | One function, many inputs, results in order |
| `pool.imap_unordered(run, tasks)` | Results as they finish: progress bars, long lists |
| `pool.starmap(burn, pairs)` | A function with several arguments |
| `pool.apply_async(burn, (0.6, 1))` | Different jobs, sent one at a time |
| `Process(target=job).start()` | One long job beside your program |
| `ProcessPoolExecutor().submit(run, task)` | The same pool, `concurrent.futures` style |

::: {.muted}
When processes must talk: `Queue`, `Pipe`, `shared_memory` and `Manager`.
:::

::: {.notes}
- `Pool.map` is today's tool; "How multiprocessing works" opens it up.
- `imap` and `imap_unordered` send one task at a time unless you set `chunksize` (Demo 3 shows why that matters).
- `apply_async` and `submit` return a handle; call `.get()` or `.result()` to wait for the answer.
:::
